analysis.one_liner: Lets banks, securities firms, and insurance companies merge into single financial conglomerates.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote in any committee or on the House floor; it died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would tear down the Glass-Steagall wall that has kept banks, securities firms, and insurance companies separate since the 1930s, and create "financial holding companies" allowed to combine all three businesses under one roof [S2]. It also preempts a range of state laws that restrict those combinations, streamlines federal oversight of the new conglomerates, modernizes the Federal Home Loan Bank system, and adds a narrow financial-privacy provision [S2]. Its centerpiece is a large deregulation for big financial firms; its consumer provisions are comparatively modest [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Large bank holding companies, securities firms, and insurers that want to combine into diversified financial conglomerates. The bill repeals the Glass-Steagall bans on bank-securities affiliation [S2][S3], lets well-capitalized holding companies buy companies in any activity the Federal Reserve deems financial [S2], and overrides state anti-affiliation laws that would block the deals [S2]. Smaller wins go to community-development groups (a new microenterprise grant program) and to Federal Home Loan Bank members through expanded housing subsidies [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Big banks, securities firms, and insurers

how_it_helps.text: Repeals sections 20 and 32 of the Glass-Steagall Act, ending the 1933-era prohibition on banks affiliating with securities firms and on interlocking directors between banks and securities houses.

Creates financial holding companies that may engage in lending, insurance underwriting and sales, securities underwriting, and other activities the Federal Reserve determines to be financial in nature, without prior approval for most activities.

Conditions that expanded power on the company's banks being well capitalized, well managed, and holding at least a 'satisfactory' Community Reinvestment Act rating, tying conglomerate expansion to performance in lending to communities.

Establishes a microenterprise technical assistance grant program for disadvantaged entrepreneurs, including those on Indian reservations, and expands Federal Home Loan Bank affordable-housing subsidies for low- and moderate-income lending.

Makes it a federal crime to obtain a bank customer's financial information under false pretenses, and requires consumer-protection rules for banks selling insurance, including disclosures that the products are not FDIC-insured.

analysis.who_pays: Depositors and federal deposit insurance funds bear the risk if newly combined bank-securities-insurance conglomerates fail, since the change extends the federally insured deposit base into riskier activities. Consumers also lose some state-level protections: the bill preempts state laws restricting bank-insurance affiliations and requires states not to regulate banks' insurance sales more harshly than other sellers [S2]. Federal Reserve oversight of nonbank subsidiaries is narrowed, with regulators barred from imposing capital requirements on subsidiaries that meet another regulator's rules [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Depositors, the deposit-insurance system, and consumers

drawbacks.text: The central change repeals the Glass-Steagall separation that kept federally insured banks out of securities underwriting, shifting more financial risk toward the government-backed deposit safety net.

The bill preempts state anti-affiliation laws and restricts states from regulating banks' insurance activities in ways that treat banks differently from other insurers, narrowing state consumer-protection authority.

Financial privacy protection is narrow: it prohibits obtaining customer information by false pretenses but imposes no general consent or opt-out requirement for sharing customers' financial data, and it directs further FTC study instead of broader rules.

It newly acquired banks can be excluded from Community Reinvestment Act community-lending requirements for roughly two years after acquisition, a gap that applies during exactly the period when a conglomerate is digesting a purchase.

The bill limits the Federal Reserve's ability to impose capital requirements on nonbank subsidiaries that satisfy any other regulator's capital rules, a constraint on one of the main tools for containing conglomerate risk.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design gives a large structural concession to the biggest financial firms and attaches comparatively small consumer benefits: a narrow anti-pretexting privacy rule, insurance-sales disclosure requirements, a CRA eligibility gate, and microenterprise grants. An honest supporter would acknowledge that the main effect is consolidating financial power, that deposit insurance ends up implicitly standing behind more complex firms, and that the privacy provision does far less than comprehensive data-sharing rules would. The Community Reinvestment Act condition and the prohibition on banks underwriting title insurance are genuine consumer-protective counterweights, but they do not change the bill's overall direction.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the last weeks of the session, sent to two House committees, and referred to a Commerce subcommittee in early November 1998; no committee vote or floor vote ever happened before the Congress expired in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. James Leach introduced the Financial Services Act of 1998 on October 20, 1998, with seven original cosponsors, all Republicans.
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Banking and Financial Services and to the Committee on Commerce.
On November 6, 1998, the Commerce Committee referred it to the Subcommittee on Finance and Hazardous Materials.
No further action is recorded; the bill was never reported out of committee and never received a floor vote before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.
The bill would have repealed the Glass-Steagall restrictions on bank-securities affiliation and created financial holding companies combining banking, securities, and insurance activities.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: In the short run, no one moved: the existing legal walls between banks, securities firms, and insurers stayed up for another year. The large financial firms seeking the change lost nothing in the long run, because an overhaul on the same theme, the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, became law the following Congress in 1999.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big financial conglomerates, which won soon after

for.what_they_did: Publicly disputed which regulator would oversee combined bank-securities-insurance firms, a standoff that stalled financial-modernization legislation in the 105th Congress and contributed to the last-minute restart this bill represented.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists; what the record shows is a Republican sponsor and seven Republican cosponsors, with no recorded Democratic support [S3][S4].

industries.industry: Large banks and bank holding companies
industries.note: The bill lets well-capitalized banking companies become financial holding companies combining banking with securities and insurance, dismantling the Depression-era separation. Ordinary depositors end up with the federal deposit-insurance safety net implicitly standing behind larger, more complex firms.

Repealing Glass-Steagall lets securities firms affiliate with banks and access insured deposits and the bank customer base. Consumers could get one-stop financial services, but at the cost of thinner separation between banking and securities risk-taking.

Insurers gain the right to affiliate with and own banks, with state anti-affiliation laws preempted, but the bill simultaneously bars national banks from underwriting title insurance and most insurance as principal, shielding insurers from bank competition in those lines.

The bill prohibits national banks and their subsidiaries from selling or underwriting title insurance, except for banks already doing it, keeping a cheaper or broader competitor out of the market and preserving insurers' pricing position over homebuyers.

industries.industry: Community banks and small financial institutions
industries.note: The bill requires a government study of its projected economic impact on institutions with assets of $100 million or less, an acknowledgment that consolidation and affiliation would pressure small institutions. It also allows community banks broader Federal Home Loan Bank advances for small-business and low-income lending.
